anomaly_def.Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a highly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, inflating resource consumption per statement.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive or apply WAL / redo records at the rate the primary produces them, causing widening replication lag.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is saturated in bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, throttling database reads and writes.

When all three surface together, the database exhibits extreme and hard-to-diagnose slowdown: suddenly changed plans trigger large table scans, hash spills, or explosion of nested-loop iterations that issue far more physical I/O and generate excessive redo. The bloated I/O stream collides with an already-constrained storage subsystem, driving up queue depths and latency on both data and log devices. As commit latency grows, the primary’s WAL archive accumulates, replicas fall minutes to hours behind, their replay workers stall on the same saturated disks, and read-only workloads on replicas see stale or inconsistent data. Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in logical I/O from plan churn, physical I/O wait from device saturation, and steep climbs in replication send, write, and replay lag, making it unclear which layer is primary.

Causally, a bad plan magnifies data-page and log traffic, pushing the storage layer past its throughput ceiling. Prolonged storage saturation lengthens commit times and slows WAL shipping, directly aggravating replication lag. In turn, the replica’s delayed apply holds WAL segments open on the primary, preventing log recycling and forcing yet more physical writes to already bottlenecked volumes. The feedback loop—poor plan → excess I/O → storage saturation → replication backlog → retained WAL → further I/O pressure—creates a self-reinforcing degradation that compromises both OLTP responsiveness and analytical query SLAs.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
